Pure cross-diffusion models:
Implications for traveling wave solutions

F. Berezovskaya Note: e-mail: fberezovskaya@howard.edu    G. Karev Affiliation: National Institutes of Health, 8600 Rockville Pike, Bethesda, MD 20894 USA    A. Novozhilov Affiliation: National Institutes of Health, 8600 Rockville Pike, Bethesda, MD 20894 USA Affiliation: Howard University, 66 Str., Washington, DC 20059 USA
Abstract

An analysis of traveling wave solutions of pure cross-diffusion systems, i.e., systems that lack reaction and self-diffusion terms, is presented. Using the qualitative theory of phase plane analysis the conditions for existence of different types of wave solutions are formulated. In particular, it is shown that family of wave trains is a generic phenomenon in pure cross-diffusion systems. The results can be used for construction and analysis of different mathematical models describing systems with directional movement.

Keywords:

PDE systems, cross-diffusion, traveling waves, traveling trains, taxis

AMS (MOS) subject classification:

34C05, 34C25, 35Q80, 92C17

1 Introduction

Using so-called cross-diffusion terms in mathematical models in natural sciences, in particular in biology, is nowadays a routine trick to incorporate into classical models additional effects such as taxis movement, crowding, pursuit, or evasion (for a review see [18]). Two particular examples, which received especial attention amongst other models, are the Keller–Segel model of chemotactic movement [17, 12, 10] (taxis is defined as behavioral response to a directional stimulus), and the Lotka–Volterra type cross-diffusion model to describe predator pursuit of an evading prey [13, 11, 7, 9].

A distinct feature of many studies on cross-diffusion models (PDE systems where diffusion matrix is not diagonal) is that usually a particular model is analyzed, where terms of reaction and diffusion coefficients are given in fixed explicit form; notable exceptions are given by [3, 10, 5]. It also appears that almost all the models considered contain reaction terms, only one exception we know of notwithstanding [8], although it might be argued that systems without reaction terms possess numerous solutions which may be relevant in biological modeling.

Taking a step further, in this note we consider the systems that lack the self-diffusion terms; PDE systems we analyze possess only cross-diffusion (as, e.g., in [6, 14], but with nonlinear cross-diffusion coefficients). We dub such systems without reaction and self-diffusion terms pure cross-diffusion systems. In particular, we study the PDE system in the following form:

ut=d1​(f⁡(u,v)​vx)x,vt=d2​(g⁡(u,v)​ux)x,\begin{split}u_{t}&=d_{1}(f(u,v)v_{x})_{x},\\ v_{t}&=d_{2}(g(u,v)u_{x})_{x},\end{split} (1)

where u=u⁡(x,t),v=v⁡(x,t),−∞<x<∞,t⩾0,u=u(x,t),\,v=v(x,t),\,-\infty<x<\infty,\,t\geqslant 0, d1,d2d_{1},d_{2} are real constants, and f⁡(u,v),g⁡(u,v)f(u,v),\,g(u,v) are arbitrary functions whose properties will be specified later. Qualitatively system (1) describes mutually dependent movement of conserved entities uu and vv on gradients of their respective counterparts. Of particular interest for us are the traveling wave solutions of system (1), which, e.g., can describe a replacement process of one species by another species. As usual, a wave solution of (1) is a bounded solution having the form u⁡(x,t)=u⁡(x+c​t)=u⁡(ξ),v⁡(x,t)=v⁡(x+c​t)=v⁡(ξ)u(x,t)=u(x+ct)=u(\xi),\,v(x,t)=v(x+ct)=v(\xi), where cc is the wave speed. On substituting these traveling wave forms into (1) we obtain the ODE wave system

c​uξ=d1​(f⁡(u,v)​vξ)ξ,c​vξ=d2​(g⁡(u,v)​uξ)ξ.\begin{split}cu_{\xi}&=d_{1}(f(u,v)v_{\xi})_{\xi},\\ cv_{\xi}&=d_{2}(g(u,v)u_{\xi})_{\xi}.\end{split} (2)

Note that we can integrate system (2), and therefore, (2) is essentially two dimensional, as the original PDE system. Each wave solution of (1) has its counterpart as a bounded orbit of (2), which, due to the particular structure of (2), is an orbit on a phase plane. There is a known correspondence between wave solutions of (1) and bounded orbits of (2): A wave front in, e.g., uu component corresponds to a heteroclinic orbit of (2) that connects singular points with different uu coordinates; A wave impulse in, e.g., uu component corresponds to a heteroclinic orbit of (1) that connects singular points with identical uu coordinates or to a homoclinic curve of a singular point; A wave train corresponds to a closed orbit of system (2).

In the next section we show that, under some natural restrictions on functions f⁡(u,v)f(u,v) and g⁡(u,v)g(u,v), all possible traveling wave solutions of (1) can be classified. In particular, a family of wave trains of (1) is a generic phenomenon intrinsic to (1). Section 3 provides some examples and extensions. Section 4 is devoted to discussion and conclusions.

2 Wave solutions of the separable models

In this note we confine ourselves to a particular case of (1), whereby the functions f⁡(u,v)f(u,v) and g⁡(u,v)g(u,v) can be represented as products of functions that depend on one variable:

f⁡(u,v)=f1​(u)​f2​(v),g⁡(u,v)=g1​(u)​g2​(v).f(u,v)=f_{1}(u)f_{2}(v),\,g(u,v)=g_{1}(u)g_{2}(v). (3)

Here the functions fi​(x),gi​(x),i=1,2f_{i}(x),\,g_{i}(x),\,i=1,2 are smooth or rational. The models of the form (1) for which (3) holds will be termed separable pure cross diffusion models, or separable models for short.

The rationale behind the choice of the from of the functions ff and gg as in (3) is twofold. Firstly, such assumption allows complete analysis of possible structures of the corresponding wave system, and thus, exhaustive classification of possible wave solutions of (1) as was done for different models in [5, 4]. Secondly, such forms are abundant in the modeling literature being the consequence of a biased random walk on the lattice (see, e.g., [16]).

For the separable model and after integration and rearrangement wave system (2) takes the form

uξ=c​d2​(v−η)/g⁡(u,v),vξ=c​d1​(u−μ)/f⁡(u,v),\begin{split}u_{\xi}&=cd_{2}(v-\eta)/g(u,v),\\ v_{\xi}&=cd_{1}(u-\mu)/f(u,v),\end{split} (4)

where c​η,c​μc\eta,\,c\mu are constants of integration that in general depend on boundary conditions, and which are considered here as new parameters of the system (see also [5]). After the change of independent variable

d​ζ=c​d​ξd1​d2​f​(u,v)​g​(u,v),d\zeta=\frac{cd\xi}{d_{1}d_{2}f(u,v)g(u,v)}\,,

which is well defined and smooth for any (u,v)(u,v) except where f⁡(u,v)​g​(u,v)=0f(u,v)g(u,v)=0 or where f⁡(u,v)f(u,v) or g⁡(u,v)g(u,v) are not defined (see [1]), we obtain

uζ=d1​f1​(u)​f2​(v)​(v−η),vζ=d2​g1​(u)​g2​(v)​(u−μ).\begin{split}u_{\zeta}&=d_{1}f_{1}(u)f_{2}(v)(v-\eta),\\ v_{\zeta}&=d_{2}g_{1}(u)g_{2}(v)(u-\mu).\end{split} (5)

In the case if f⁡(u,v)f(u,v) or g⁡(u,v)g(u,v) are rational, the change of independent variable is chosen such that the resulting wave system is well defined for all uu, vv (for examples see the next section). Therefore, without loss of generality, we assume that our wave system has the form

uζ=d1​φ1​(u)​φ2​(v)​(v−η),vζ=d2​ψ1​(u)​ψ2​(v)​(u−μ).\begin{split}u_{\zeta}&=d_{1}\varphi_{1}(u)\varphi_{2}(v)(v-\eta),\\ v_{\zeta}&=d_{2}\psi_{1}(u)\psi_{2}(v)(u-\mu).\end{split} (6)

which is defined for all u,vu,\,v.

First we note that system (6) is integrable. Function

H⁡(u,v)=d1​∫(v−η)​φ2​(v)ψ2​(v)​𝑑v−d2​∫(u−μ)​ψ1​(u)φ1​(u)​𝑑u+constH(u,v)=d_{1}\int(v-\eta)\frac{\varphi_{2}(v)}{\psi_{2}(v)}\,dv-{d_{2}}\int(u-\mu)\frac{\psi_{1}(u)}{\varphi_{1}(u)}\,du+\mbox{const}

represents its integral. We remark that under the assumption φ1​(u)=const,ψ2​(v)=const\varphi_{1}(u)=\mbox{const},\,\psi_{2}(v)=\mbox{const} system (6) is hamiltonian, and H⁡(u,v)H(u,v) is its Hamiltonian, which automatically yields that the singular points of (6) can be only topological saddles or centers.

We assume that the following conditions of non-degeneracy are fulfilled (these conditions are natural as far as we consider η,μ,c\eta,\,\mu,\,c the only parameters in the system (6)):

(C​1)φ1​(u) and ψ1​(u) have no common roots;(C​2)φ2​(v) and ψ2​(v) have no common roots;(C​3)φi​(x) and ψi​(x),i=1,2, have no multiple roots.\begin{split}(C1)&\quad\mbox{$\varphi_{1}(u)$ and $\psi_{1}(u)$ have no common roots;}\\ (C2)&\quad\mbox{$\varphi_{2}(v)$ and $\psi_{2}(v)$ have no common roots;}\\ (C3)&\quad\mbox{$\varphi_{i}(x)$ and $\psi_{i}(x),\,i=1,2,$ have no multiple roots.}\end{split}

System (6) always has singular point (μ,η)(\mu,\,\eta). Coordinates of other singular points are (μ,v^i),(u^i,η),(u^i,v^i)(\mu,\hat{v}_{i}),\,(\hat{u}_{i},\,\eta),\,(\hat{u}_{i},\hat{v}_{i}), where u^i\hat{u}_{i} and v^i\hat{v}_{i} are the solutions of one of the systems:

φ1​(u)=0,ψ2​(v)=0,\varphi_{1}(u)=0,\quad\psi_{2}(v)=0, (7)

or

φ2​(v)=0,ψ1​(u)=0.\varphi_{2}(v)=0,\quad\psi_{1}(u)=0. (8)

To infer the possible types of the singular points of (6) consider the Jacobi matrix of (6): D​F​(u,v)=(ai​j)2×2,i,j=1,2DF(u,v)=(a_{ij})_{2\times 2},\,i,j=1,2:

a11=d1​(v−η)​φ2​(v)​(φ1​(u))u′,a12=d1​φ1​(u)​((v−η)​(φ2​(v))v′+φ2​(v)),a21=d2​ϕ2​(v)​((u−μ)​(ψ1​(u))u′+ψ1​(u)),a22=d2​(u−μ)​ψ1​(u)​(ψ2​(v))v′.\begin{split}a_{11}&=d_{1}(v-\eta)\varphi_{2}(v)(\varphi_{1}(u))^{\prime}_{u},\\ a_{12}&=d_{1}\varphi_{1}(u)((v-\eta)(\varphi_{2}(v))^{\prime}_{v}+\varphi_{2}(v)),\\ a_{21}&=d_{2}\phi_{2}(v)((u-\mu)(\psi_{1}(u))^{\prime}_{u}+\psi_{1}(u)),\\ a_{22}&=d_{2}(u-\mu)\psi_{1}(u)(\psi_{2}(v))^{\prime}_{v}.\end{split} (9)

Direct substitution of singular point coordinates into (9) and evaluation of trace and determinant of D​FDF implies the following proposition.

Proposition 1.

Let us assume that conditions (C​1)(C1)–(C​3)(C3) hold. We also assume that u^i\hat{u}_{i} (v^i\hat{v}_{i}) do not coincide with μ\mu (η\eta, respectively). Then

1. Singular points of (6) satisfying (7) or (8) can be saddles or nodes only;

2. Singular points of (6) where one or both coordinates are η\eta or μ\mu can be centers or saddles only.

Remark 1.

If we relax condition (C​3)(C3) retaining (C​1)(C1) and (C​2)(C2) then we have to add to the list of possible singular points of (6) saddle-node points.

Remark 2.

To prove that singular points that have eigenvalues with zero real part in linear approximation are indeed centers we can use integrability of system (6) and Theorem 2 in [2, p. 75].

From Proposition 1, integrability of system (6), and special structure of the wave system (6) follows that the structure of the phase plane, and, consequently, of the bounded orbits of (6) are completely determined by the types and mutual positions of singular points of (6). The phase plane is divided into orbit cells that represent either a rectangular cell with orbit structure determined by the types of the corner singular points (as in [5]), or a cell filled with closed orbits surrounding singular point of the center type (an example of such phase plane is given in Fig. 1). The former case corresponds to fronts or impulses of the initial system (1), and the latter to the wave train solutions of system (1).

Summarizing, we obtain the basic result of the present note:

Theorem 1.

The separable pure cross-diffusion system (1), satisfying (C​1)(C1)–(C​3)(C3) can only possess traveling wave solutions of the following kinds: i. impulse-front solutions; ii. front-front solutions; iii. impulse-impulse solutions; iv. family of wave train solutions.

The family of wave train solutions exits in domain Ω\Omega if f⁡(u,v)f(u,v) and g⁡(u,v)g(u,v) are analytical in Ω\Omega and d1​d2​f​(u,v)​g​(u,v)<0d_{1}d_{2}f(u,v)g(u,v)<0 for (u,v)∈Ω(u,v)\in\Omega.

3 Examples

Example 1.

The simplest possible separable model (1) is obtained if we put

f1​(u)=f2​(v)=g1​(u)=g2​(v)=1.f_{1}(u)=f_{2}(v)=g_{1}(u)=g_{2}(v)=1. (10)

The integral in this case is given by

d2​(u−μ)2−d1​(v−η)2=const.d_{2}(u-\mu)^{2}-d_{1}(v-\eta)^{2}=\mbox{const}.

From which it follows that system (1) with (10) has no traveling wave solution if d1​d2>0d_{1}d_{2}>0 and has a family of traveling trains if d1​d2<0d_{1}d_{2}<0.

Remark.

Note that in case d1​d2<0d_{1}d_{2}<0 system (1) is equivalent to the beam equation ut​t=−D​ux​x​x​x,D>0u_{tt}=-Du_{xxxx},\,D>0, which, how it is well known, possesses wave solutions.

Example 2.

Let

f2​(v)=g1​(u)=constf1​(u)=(u−a)n,g2(v)=(v−b)m,n,m∈ℕ.\begin{split}f_{2}(v)&=g_{1}(u)=\mbox{const}\\ f_{1}(u)&=(u-a)^{n},\,g_{2}(v)=(v-b)^{m},\,n,m\in\mathbb{N}.\end{split} (11)

It is straightforward to prove

Proposition 2.

Separable model (1) with (11) has a family of wave trains if d1​d2<0d_{1}d_{2}<0 and has a front-front solution, that corresponds to a heteroclinic connecting node and saddle, if d1​d2>0d_{1}d_{2}>0.

Example 3.

Let

f1​(u)=un,f2(v)=1vm,g1​(u)=1un,g2(v)=vm,\begin{split}f_{1}(u)&=u^{n},\,f_{2}(v)=\frac{1}{v^{m}}\,,\\ g_{1}(u)&=\frac{1}{u^{n}}\,,\,g_{2}(v)=v^{m},\end{split} (12)

where m,n∈ℕm,n\in\mathbb{N}. After a suitably chosen change of independent variable in the wave system (4) we obtain

uζ=d1​u2​n​(v−η),vζ=d2​v2​m​(u−μ).\begin{split}u_{\zeta}&=d_{1}u^{2n}(v-\eta),\\ v_{\zeta}&=d_{2}v^{2m}(u-\mu).\end{split} (13)

Having in mind biological applications of the pure cross-diffusion models we assume that μ>0,η>0\mu>0,\,\eta>0 and analyze the phase plane in the first quadrant. System (13) has two singular points: (0,0)(0,0) and (μ,η)(\mu,\,\eta). The point (μ,η)(\mu,\,\eta) can be a saddle (if d1​d2>0d_{1}d_{2}>0) or a center (d1​d2<0d_{1}d_{2}<0). If we restrict our attention only to the cases μ>0,η>0\mu>0,\,\eta>0, u,v>0u,v>0, then traveling wave solutions of (1) with (13) are exactly the same as in Proposition 2.

Let us illustrate this case. In Fig. 2 the first quadrant of the phase plane of the wave system of (1),(12) is shown for two topologically nonequivalent cases. The first case corresponds to the wave train in the original PDE system, and the second case corresponds to front-front solution. In Fig. 3 numerically obtained solutions of (1),(12) are presented. To approximate cross-diffusion term an “upwind” explicit scheme was used [15] which is often used for cross-diffusion systems (e.g., [19]).

Example 4.

We can use obtained results to prove existence of solutions of a special form when simple reaction terms are presented. For example, let us consider the following system:

ut=b1​u+d1​(un/vm​vx)x,vt=b2​v+d2​(vm/un​ux)x.\begin{split}u_{t}&=b_{1}u+d_{1}(u^{n}/v^{m}v_{x})_{x},\\ v_{t}&=b_{2}v+d_{2}(v^{m}/u^{n}u_{x})_{x}.\end{split} (14)

If the constant b1,b2,n,mb_{1},\,b_{2},\,n,\,m satisfy the following equality:

b1​(1−n)=b2​(1−m),b_{1}(1-n)=b_{2}(1-m),

then by the change

u⁡(x,t)=eb1​t​z​(z,t),v⁡(x,t)=eb2​t​w​(x,t)u(x,t)=e^{b_{1}t}z(z,t),\,v(x,t)=e^{b_{2}t}w(x,t)

system (14) can be reduced to system (1), (12). Thus system (14) has wave train solutions with amplitude changing with time. It is interesting to note that for some models of the form (14) an exact solution can be found.

Example 5.

Consider the system

ut=u+d1​vx​x,vt=−γ​v+d2​ux​x.\begin{split}u_{t}&=u+d_{1}v_{xx},\\ v_{t}&=-\gamma v+d_{2}u_{xx}.\end{split} (15)
Proposition 3.

For γ<1\gamma<1 and d1+d2>0d_{1}+d_{2}>0 system (15) has a family of wave trains.

Proof.

We will prove proposition by presenting a solution of (15) in explicit form.

Let u⁡(ξ)=cos⁡k​ξ,v⁡(ξ)=sin⁡k​ξ,ξ=x+c​tu(\xi)=\cos k\xi,\,v(\xi)=\sin k\xi,\,\xi=x+ct. Then system (15) transforms to the equations

−c​k​sin⁡k​ξ=sin⁡k​ξ−d1​k2​sin⁡k​ξ,c​k​cos⁡k​ξ=−γ​cos⁡k​ξ−d2​k2​cos⁡k​ξ,\begin{split}-ck\sin k\xi&=\sin k\xi-d_{1}k^{2}\sin k\xi,\\ ck\cos k\xi&=-\gamma\cos k\xi-d_{2}k^{2}\cos k\xi,\end{split}

from which

d1​k2−c​k−1=0,d2​k2+c​k+γ=0\begin{split}d_{1}k^{2}-ck-1&=0,\\ d_{2}k^{2}+ck+\gamma&=0\end{split}

follows. For fixed d1,d2,γd_{1},\,d_{2},\,\gamma the solution of the last system is given by

k=1−γd1+d2,c=−d2+d1​γ(d1+d2)​(1−γ),k=\frac{\sqrt{1-\gamma}}{d_{1}+d_{2}},\,c=-\frac{d_{2}+d_{1}\gamma}{\sqrt{(d_{1}+d_{2})(1-\gamma)}},

which is defined for γ<1\gamma<1 and d1+d2>0d_{1}+d_{2}>0, which completes the proof. ∎

Example 6.

An obvious question is what kind of solutions can appear in pure cross-diffusion models if we do not demand that the functions f⁡(u,v)f(u,v) and g⁡(u,v)g(u,v) can be represented as the product of functions of one variable. Despite the fact that the separable models possess very reach structure of possible traveling wave solutions, simple extension of the models considered can be shown to yield a different type of behavior.

Consider the model (1) with the functions given by

f⁡(u,v)=uα​u+v,g⁡(u,v)=vu+β​v,\begin{split}f(u,v)&=\frac{u}{\alpha u+v},\\ g(u,v)&=\frac{v}{u+\beta v},\end{split} (16)

where α\alpha and β\beta are positive constant.

The wave system, after suitable change of independent variable, reads

uζ=d1​(v−η)​u​(α​u+η),vζ=d2​(u−μ)​v​(u+β​v).\begin{split}u_{\zeta}&=d_{1}(v-\eta)u(\alpha u+\eta),\\ v_{\zeta}&=d_{2}(u-\mu)v(u+\beta v).\end{split} (17)

Assume that all the parameters, except for d1,d2d_{1},\,d_{2} are positive. Singular point (μ,η)(\mu,\,\eta) is a saddle, if d1​d2>0d_{1}d_{2}>0 and a center at linear approximation for d1​d2<0d_{1}d_{2}<0. However, contrast to model in Example 3, and due to the fact that the wave system is now non-integrable, we cannot make conclusion on the type of the singular point in the case d1​d2<0d_{1}d_{2}<0. If we calculate the first Lyapunov value l1l_{1} [2], we obtain l1=d1​d2​μ​η​(α​β−1)​(α​μ2−β​η2)l_{1}=d_{1}d_{2}\mu\eta(\alpha\beta-1)(\alpha\mu^{2}-\beta\eta^{2}), which shows that for parameter values where l1≠0l_{1}\neq 0 this singular point can be either stable or unstable nonlinear focus.

Numerical experiments show that at least for some parameter values there is a limit cycle surrounding the singular point (see Fig. 4). Thus, in this example, there is a wave train solution of the initial pure cross-diffusion system.

4 Conclusions

In the present note we have shown that pure cross-diffusion models possess very rich structure of possible traveling wave solutions even in a rather simplified, though still realistic, case of separable models, when the nonlinear cross-diffusion coefficients in system (1) can be represented by product of functions depending on one variable.

A distinct feature of pure cross diffusion models is the presence, under some additional condition, of the family of wave train solutions (such solutions were not found for several classed of cross-diffusion models describing taxis, see [5, 4]). As numerical experiments show, such wave trains can be observed at least for some time interval. Together with families of wave trains, other typical cases of traveling waves can be observed. In particular, impulse-front, front-front, and impulse-impulse solutions are also a possibility.

We emphasize that the separable model (1), even when the values of parameters μ,η,c\mu,\eta,c are fixed, possesses, in general, a family of traveling wave solutions; there are infinitely many bounded orbits of (2) that correspond to traveling wave solutions.

The presented results can be used for construction and analysis of different mathematical models describing systems where directional movement is of particular importance.

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
